title: Does God Change His Mind?
lead: Several passages say God "regretted" or "relented" (Hebrew nicham), while others say he does not change his mind like a human being. Jews and Christians have read the tension in different ways: as human language for an unchanging God, as real responsiveness to people's choices, or as both at once.

sections.b: God regrets making humankind before the Flood (Genesis 6:6) and relents from destroying Israel after the golden calf when Moses prays (Exodus 32:14). Balaam says God is not a human being "that he should change his mind" (Numbers 23:19). In 1 Samuel 15 the LORD regrets making Saul king (1 Samuel 15:11; 1 Samuel 15:35), yet Samuel says Israel's God "does not regret" (1 Samuel 15:29). The prophets speak of God relenting when people turn (Jeremiah 18:7–10; Joel 2:13; Jonah 3:10; Jonah 4:2), and Malachi 3:6 says "I am the LORD, and I do not change." James 1:17 adds that with the Father of lights there is "no variation or shadow due to change," a verse classical theologians cite alongside Numbers 23:19 and 1 Samuel 15:29. Readers explain the tension as accommodation (God speaks in human terms), as a difference between God's purposes (fixed) and his dealings (responsive), or, in open theism, as real change in God's plans.
